question: Where would you first look to check exactly which tasks are part of your job?
explanation: Your job description sets out your main duties and who you report to. Agreed ways of working and policies then describe how each task is done.

question: What does the phrase "agreed ways of working" mean in a care setting?
optionA: Habits shared by the whole team
optionC: Rules each worker writes for themselves
optionD: Tips from the people you support
explanation: Agreed ways of working are the policies, procedures and guidance your employer has set out. They may be less formal in a small setting but you must still follow them.

question: Which body registers and inspects adult social care services in England?
explanation: The Care Quality Commission (CQC) registers, monitors and inspects health and adult social care services in England. Skills for Care supports workforce development but does not inspect.

question: A person you support asks you to do a task you have not been trained to do. What should you do?
optionB: Ask the person to show you how
optionC: Ask a visitor to do it instead
explanation: You must work within your competence. Explain kindly that you cannot do it yet and report to your manager so it is done safely and you can be trained.

question: Which code describes the expected behaviour of healthcare support workers and adult social care workers in England?
optionA: The Code of Conduct for support workers
optionB: The NMC Code for nurses and midwives
explanation: The Code of Conduct for Healthcare Support Workers and Adult Social Care Workers in England sets out the standards of behaviour expected. The NMC Code applies to registered nurses and midwives.

question: What is an advocate's main role for a person who uses care services?
optionB: To help them have their say
optionC: To manage their money for them
explanation: An advocate supports a person to express their views and wishes and to stand up for their rights. They do not take over decisions the person can make.

question: Why is it important to work in partnership with a person's family and friends?
explanation: Family and friends often know the person's history, preferences and routines. Working with them, with the person's agreement, gives better person-centred care.

question: You disagree with how a senior colleague does a task. What is the best first step?
optionA: Copy them so the team stays consistent
optionB: Tell the people you support about it
optionC: Post about it on social media
optionD: Raise it calmly through proper channels
explanation: Concerns about practice should be raised through agreed channels, calmly and professionally. Complaining to people who use the service or online breaks confidentiality and trust.

question: Your manager asks to meet you every few weeks to discuss your work and wellbeing. What is this meeting called?
explanation: Supervision is a regular meeting with your manager to review your practice, support you and agree development. An appraisal is usually a yearly review of performance.

question: What is a personal development plan?
optionA: A list of your shifts for the next month
optionB: Your learning goals and how to meet them
optionC: A summary of a person's care needs
optionD: A plan for a fire evacuation of the home
explanation: A personal development plan records your learning goals, how you will achieve them, the support you need and when you will review them.

question: What does reflective practice mean?
optionA: Copying how others do each care task
optionB: Writing up every task you finish
optionC: Thinking back on your work to improve
optionD: Repeating the same training every year
explanation: Reflective practice means looking back at what happened, what went well, what could be better and what you will do differently. It helps you keep improving.

question: A goal in your development plan says: "Complete moving and handling training by 30 June." Which SMART element does the date give it?
explanation: SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. The deadline makes the goal time-bound.

question: Who can give you useful feedback on your work?
optionB: Only your line manager or deputy
optionC: Only CQC inspectors on a visit
optionD: Only your trainer on a course
explanation: Feedback can come from the people you support, their families, colleagues and managers. Each sees your work from a different angle.

question: Which digital skill does a care worker most often need at work?
optionA: Building a website for the service
optionB: Recording care on a care app
explanation: Many services now keep care records electronically, so workers need to use approved digital tools safely and securely as part of their role.

question: What should you do if you receive feedback you find hard to hear?
optionA: Argue the point until it is withdrawn
optionB: Ignore it if you do not agree with it
optionC: Listen and think about how to use it
optionD: Ask to be moved to a different manager
explanation: Feedback is a chance to learn. Listen, ask questions to understand it and agree with your manager how you will act on it.

question: Your values do not match the care choice a person makes. What should guide your actions?
optionA: Your own beliefs about what is best
optionC: What is quickest for the team
optionD: The person's wishes and care plan
explanation: Person-centred practice means respecting the person's choices, as set out in their care plan, even when you would choose differently. Raise any safety worries with your manager.

question: What is continuing professional development (CPD)?
optionB: Training given only in your first week
optionC: A test you sit once each year
optionD: A pay rise given after each course
explanation: CPD is the learning you keep doing throughout your working life so your knowledge and skills stay up to date.

question: When should you ask for help with your own learning needs?
optionB: As soon as you notice a gap
optionD: Only when told to by CQC
explanation: Raise learning needs early, in supervision or before, so you are supported before a gap affects the people you care for.

question: Why must you know the limits of your role?
optionA: To avoid taking on any extra tasks
optionB: To finish every shift on time
optionC: To keep people and yourself safe
optionD: To be promoted sooner than others
explanation: Staying within your role and competence protects people from harm and protects you. Tasks outside it should be referred to the right person.

question: What could your career progress to after you complete the Care Certificate?
optionA: Nothing, it is the final step
optionB: Only a manager's job straight away
explanation: The Care Certificate is a starting point. Workers can go on to qualifications such as the Level 2 Adult Social Care Certificate and higher diplomas, and to senior or specialist roles.

question: What does a duty of care mean for a care worker?
optionB: Doing whatever people ask without question
optionC: Keeping people indoors so they stay safe
optionD: Following family wishes over the person's
explanation: A duty of care is a legal obligation to act in the best interests of the people you support and not to act, or fail to act, in a way that causes harm.

question: What is the duty of candour?
optionA: Keeping errors within the staff team
optionB: Being open when things go wrong
optionD: Sharing records with anyone who asks
explanation: Providers registered with CQC must be open and transparent with people when something goes wrong with their care, give an apology and explain what happened. Workers support this by reporting errors honestly.

question: A person with capacity wants to walk to the shop alone, but you think they might fall. What best balances their rights and your duty of care?
optionA: Lock the door until a carer is free
optionB: Refuse and record that they refused care
optionC: Talk through the risks with them
optionD: Let them go without saying anything
explanation: Duty of care does not mean removing all risk. Talk through the risks, agree safer options with the person and record and report the decision as your agreed ways of working say.

question: A person makes a complaint to you about their care. What should you do first?
optionA: Tell them to write to CQC instead
optionB: Explain that it is not your fault
optionC: Ignore it if it seems minor to you
explanation: Listen without becoming defensive, reassure the person that complaints are welcome and follow your employer's complaints procedure so it is recorded and dealt with.

question: What is a near miss?
optionA: An event that could have caused harm
optionB: An incident that caused serious harm
optionC: A task finished just before its deadline
optionD: A complaint that was later withdrawn
explanation: A near miss is an unplanned event that did not cause harm but could have. Reporting near misses helps prevent the same thing happening again.

question: You realise you gave someone the wrong drink thickness. They seem fine. What should you do?
optionA: Say nothing as no harm was done
optionB: Report and record it at once
optionD: Wait to see if symptoms appear
explanation: Errors must be reported promptly even when no harm is seen, so the person can be checked and lessons learnt. Hiding mistakes breaks your duty of care and the duty of candour.

question: A person's relative shouts at you in the corridor. What is the best response?
optionA: Shout back to stand your ground
explanation: Keep calm, listen to the concern, avoid arguing and get support from a senior colleague if the situation does not settle. Your own safety matters too.

question: Who can a person go to if they are unhappy with how a council-funded or self-funded care service handled their complaint in England?
optionC: The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
optionD: The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman
explanation: When a complaint about adult social care is not resolved by the provider, people can take it to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman. CQC wants to hear about concerns but does not resolve individual complaints.

question: What does an accident or incident report need to be?
optionB: Short, so it is quick to read
optionD: Kept by you, not the employer
explanation: Reports should state facts, not opinions, be accurate and be completed as soon as possible while details are fresh, following agreed ways of working.

question: What is the main purpose of a risk assessment in a person's care plan?
optionA: To stop every risky activity safely
optionB: To enable choices while reducing harm
optionC: To protect staff from any complaints
optionD: To decide who pays for the care
explanation: Risk assessment helps people do what matters to them as safely as possible. It is a tool for enabling choice, not for removing it.

question: Which law in Great Britain protects people from discrimination because of protected characteristics?
optionD: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
explanation: The Equality Act 2010 brings together discrimination law and lists nine protected characteristics. The Care Act deals with care and support and safeguarding.

question: How many protected characteristics does the Equality Act 2010 list?
explanation: They are age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation.

question: Which of these is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?
explanation: Religion or belief is one of the nine protected characteristics. The others include age, disability, race, sex and sexual orientation.

question: What does inclusion mean in a care setting?
optionA: Everyone gets exactly the same care
optionB: Everyone can take part and belong
explanation: Inclusion means removing barriers so each person can take part fully and feel they belong. It does not mean treating everyone identically.

question: What does treating people equally but not the same mean?
optionA: Giving every person the same meal
optionB: Using the same words with everyone
explanation: Equality is about fair outcomes. People have different needs and backgrounds, so fair care means adapting support to each person.

question: A colleague makes a joke about a resident's religion. What should you do?
optionA: Laugh so the team gets on
optionB: Ignore it if the resident is out
explanation: Discriminatory comments must not go unchallenged. Challenge them if it is safe and appropriate, and report them following your agreed ways of working.

question: Which law in the UK brings the European Convention on Human Rights into domestic law?
explanation: The Human Rights Act 1998 lets people rely on Convention rights in UK courts and requires public bodies, and in many cases care providers whose care is arranged or paid for by a council, to respect those rights.

question: Which human right is most at stake when a person is not allowed to choose their own clothes?
optionA: The right to a fair trial
optionB: Respect for private and family life
explanation: Article 8 of the Human Rights Act protects private and family life, which includes personal choices about appearance and daily routine.

question: What is unconscious bias?
optionA: Prejudice a person shows on purpose
optionB: A rule that applies to everyone
explanation: Unconscious bias is an attitude or stereotype that affects how we act without us being aware of it. Reflecting on our reactions helps reduce it.

question: A policy says all residents must have a bath, not a shower. Whom could this disadvantage?
optionA: People who prefer to eat in the evening
optionD: People whose faith needs running water
explanation: A rule applied to everyone can put some groups at a disadvantage, for example people whose religion requires washing in running water. This can be indirect discrimination.

question: How can you provide culturally appropriate care?
optionA: Ask the person about their customs
optionB: Assume customs from their country of birth
optionD: Treat every person in the same way
explanation: Ask the person, and those close to them if they agree, about their culture, faith, diet and preferences. Assumptions based on background can be wrong.

question: What is direct discrimination?
optionA: A rule that affects one group more
optionB: Treating someone worse for who they are
optionD: Giving extra help to a disabled person
explanation: Direct discrimination is treating a person less favourably because of a protected characteristic. A rule that puts one group at a disadvantage is indirect discrimination.

question: Where can a care worker find reliable information about equality and human rights?
explanation: Agreed ways of working, managers and official bodies such as the Equality and Human Rights Commission give reliable information and support.

question: What should you do if you see a colleague refusing to support a resident because of their sexual orientation?
optionA: Leave it, as it is their view
optionC: Raise it only if it happens again
explanation: Refusing care because of sexual orientation is discrimination. Report it through agreed ways of working so the person is protected and the behaviour is addressed.

question: What is person-centred care?
optionB: Care planned around the staff rota
optionC: Care that is the same for everyone
optionD: Care decided mainly by the family
explanation: Person-centred care puts the individual at the centre, with care shaped by their needs, preferences, history and choices.

question: Which of these is a person-centred value?
explanation: Person-centred values include individuality, independence, privacy, partnership, choice, dignity, respect and rights.

question: Where should you find out how a person likes to be supported?
optionB: The handover sheet from last week
optionC: Their care plan and the person
explanation: The care plan records the person's needs and preferences, and the person themselves is the best source of what they want today.

question: A person who usually has a shower says they want a wash at the sink today. What should you do?
optionA: Insist on the shower as planned
optionC: Ask their family to persuade them
optionD: Respect the choice and record it
explanation: People can change their minds. Respect the choice, support the wash and record it; report any pattern that may affect health.

question: Which law sets out how to support people who may lack mental capacity in England and Wales?
explanation: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 sets out how to assess capacity and make decisions in a person's best interests. The Mental Health Act covers assessment and treatment of mental disorder, including detention.

question: What is the first principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005?
explanation: A person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it. Age, appearance or diagnosis alone never prove a lack of capacity.

question: Under the Mental Capacity Act, a person makes a choice that others think is unwise. What does this mean?
optionA: They must lack capacity for that choice
optionC: It does not prove they lack capacity
optionD: Their family takes over the decision
explanation: One of the five principles is that a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because it is unwise.

question: Capacity is assessed for what?
optionA: All decisions for the rest of life
optionB: All decisions for the next month
explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. A person may be able to choose what to wear but not to manage complex finances, and capacity can change.

question: Which of these is part of the Mental Capacity Act's test of whether a person can make a decision?
optionB: Can they read and write in English?
optionC: Do they agree with staff advice?
explanation: A person is unable to decide if they cannot understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it, or communicate their decision.

question: If a decision is made for a person who lacks capacity, how must it be made?
explanation: Decisions made for a person who lacks capacity must be in their best interests and should be the option least restrictive of their rights and freedom.

question: What can a lasting power of attorney do?
optionA: Let staff decide all of the care
optionB: Let a doctor manage the person's money
optionC: Let a chosen person decide for them
optionD: Let the council sell the person's home
explanation: A lasting power of attorney is made while a person has capacity. It names who can make health and welfare or property and financial decisions if they later lose capacity.

question: What should you do before giving personal care?
optionA: Start quickly to save them time
optionB: Ask a colleague to give consent
optionC: Ask the family for consent each time
optionD: Explain and get the person's consent
explanation: Valid consent is needed before any care or support. Explain what you plan to do in a way the person understands and check they agree.

question: A person refuses to take part in an activity they usually enjoy. What should you do?
optionA: Respect it and gently ask why
optionD: Remove the activity from the plan
explanation: People have the right to refuse. Respect the decision and gently explore the reason, which may point to pain, low mood or another need to report.

question: What does supporting a person's independence mean?
optionA: Doing tasks for them to save effort
optionB: Helping them do what they can
optionC: Leaving them alone most of the day
explanation: Supporting independence means encouraging people to do as much as they can, with the right help, so they keep skills and confidence.

question: Which of these could show that a person is in pain but cannot say so?
optionA: Asking for a cup of tea
explanation: Signs of pain include facial expressions, guarding, changes in posture, restlessness, withdrawal or new distress. Report them so pain can be assessed.

question: A person seems withdrawn and tearful. What should you do?
optionA: Leave them alone until it passes
optionB: Tell them to try to cheer up
optionC: Record it only if it lasts a month
explanation: Emotional distress matters as much as physical pain. Offer comfort, listen and report changes so their wellbeing can be supported.

question: How can you support a person's wellbeing?
optionA: Help them keep up what matters
optionB: Keep their days the same as others'
explanation: Wellbeing includes feeling valued, connected and able to do things that matter, such as faith, hobbies, relationships and routines.

question: What is a life history or one-page profile used for?
explanation: Life story work and one-page profiles help staff understand what is important to the person and how best to support them.

question: You are about to help someone wash. What protects their privacy?
optionA: Leave the door open for air
optionB: Chat with colleagues in the room
explanation: Closing doors and curtains and keeping parts of the body covered when not being washed protect privacy and dignity.

question: What should you do before entering a person's bedroom?
optionA: Walk straight in if the door is shut
optionB: Knock as you open the door
optionD: Knock and wait for an answer
explanation: A person's room is their private space. Knock and wait for an answer, or follow their agreed preference if they cannot answer.

question: What does dignity mean in care?
optionB: Giving care as fast as possible
optionC: Using pet names to be friendly
explanation: Dignity means treating people with respect, as individuals whose choices, privacy and feelings matter.

question: A person wants to be called by their title and surname. What should you do?
optionA: Use their first name to be friendly
explanation: Use the name the person chooses. Terms like "love" or "dear" can feel patronising and undermine dignity.

question: You need to discuss a person's continence care with a colleague. Where should you do it?
explanation: Personal information should be discussed where others cannot overhear, to protect privacy and confidentiality.

question: A person's family want them to stop seeing a friend from church. The person has capacity and wants to keep seeing them. What should happen?
optionB: Stop the visits for a trial
explanation: A person with capacity has the right to decide who they see. Supporting relationships and community links is part of dignity and wellbeing.

question: How can you support a person to stay part of their community?
optionA: Help them keep up local links
optionB: Plan all activities inside the home
optionD: Limit trips to save staff time
explanation: Community links such as clubs, faith groups and friends support wellbeing and independence. Follow the person's choices.

question: When is it right to share information about a person's personal care with others?
optionA: When visitors ask how the person is
optionB: When they need to know to give care
explanation: Share personal information only on a need-to-know basis, with people involved in the person's care, following agreed ways of working.

question: A person with mobility needs prefers to dress slowly by themselves. The morning is busy. What should you do?
optionA: Dress them to keep to schedule
optionB: Ask them to stay in nightwear
optionC: Give them time to dress themselves
optionD: Dress them and record it as their choice
explanation: Taking over to save time removes independence and dignity. Support the person at their pace and raise staffing pressure with your manager.

question: Which of these is a way to respect a person's dignity at mealtimes?
optionA: Feed them quickly to keep to time
optionB: Put aprons on everyone at the table
optionC: Stand over them while helping them eat
optionD: Offer choice and go at their pace
explanation: Offer choices, sit at the person's level if helping them eat, go at their pace and use protective clothing only if they want it.

question: What should you do if you see a colleague leave a person exposed during personal care?
optionA: Cover the person and report it
optionC: Wait until the end of the shift
optionD: Mention it to the person's visitor
explanation: Protect the person straight away, then report it through agreed ways of working. Ignoring poor practice can allow it to continue.

question: What is meant by active participation?
optionA: Staff take charge of all the tasks
optionB: The person shares in their own care
optionD: The person joins a group exercise class
explanation: Active participation means the person is a partner in their care and daily life, not a passive recipient.

question: Which question best supports a person to make their own choice about clothes?
optionA: You'll wear this one, won't you?
optionC: Which would you like to wear?
explanation: Offering real options in a clear, open way supports choice. Leading questions or choosing for the person take control away.

question: Why should you not discuss one resident's care in front of another?
optionA: It wastes too much staff time
optionB: It may create a fire risk
explanation: Talking about someone's care where others can hear breaches their privacy and confidentiality and can cause embarrassment.

question: Which of these is non-verbal communication?
explanation: Non-verbal communication includes facial expressions, gestures, body language, eye contact and touch.

question: What is active listening?
optionA: Talking while the person is still speaking
optionB: Focusing fully and checking you understood
optionC: Writing notes without any eye contact
optionD: Planning your reply while they talk
explanation: Active listening means focusing on the speaker, showing interest, letting them finish and checking back what they meant.

question: A person who wears a hearing aid seems not to follow you. What should you check first?
optionA: That the TV is turned up loudly
optionC: That the aid is in and working
explanation: Check the hearing aid is fitted, switched on, clean and has a working battery. Then face the person, reduce background noise and speak clearly.

question: How should you speak to a person with hearing loss who lip-reads?
optionA: Shout clearly from across the room
optionB: Cover your mouth to be polite
explanation: Face the person with light on your face, speak clearly at a normal pace and do not exaggerate lip movements or shout.

question: What is Makaton?
optionA: Signs and symbols used with speech
optionB: A type of digital hearing aid
optionD: A sign language used in Wales
explanation: Makaton uses signs and symbols alongside speech to support people who have difficulty communicating, such as some people with a learning disability.

question: What does it mean that behaviour can be a form of communication?
optionB: Actions can show needs or feelings
optionD: Behaviour is never linked to needs
explanation: A change in behaviour, such as agitation or withdrawal, may be how a person shows pain, fear, boredom or another need they cannot put into words.

question: Which standard requires health and adult social care services in England to meet the communication needs of disabled people?
explanation: The Accessible Information Standard requires NHS and publicly funded adult social care services to identify, record, flag, share and meet people's information and communication needs.

question: What is an example of assistive technology for communication?
explanation: Communication aids range from picture boards to tablets and devices that speak typed or chosen words.

question: A person speaks little English. What is the best way to discuss their care?
optionD: Ask a passing visitor to help
explanation: A trained interpreter gives accurate, confidential communication. Using children or untrained people risks errors and breaches privacy.

question: Which of these is a barrier to communication?
explanation: Noise, poor lighting, jargon, distractions and unfamiliar language are common barriers. Reduce them before an important conversation.

question: Which question is open?
explanation: Open questions invite fuller answers. Closed questions, answered yes or no, are useful for people who find long replies hard.

question: What is meant by confidentiality in care?
optionB: Sharing only with the person's friends
explanation: Confidential information is shared only with those who need it to give care, with consent where possible, or when there is a legal or safety reason.

question: When may you share confidential information without the person's consent?
optionA: When someone is at risk of harm
optionB: When a relative phones to ask
explanation: Confidentiality can be overridden to protect someone from serious harm, such as in a safeguarding concern. Follow agreed ways of working and tell your manager.

question: Which laws govern how personal data is handled in the UK?
optionA: The Care Act 2014 and the Children Act
optionB: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act
optionC: The Equality Act and Human Rights Act
explanation: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 set the rules for collecting, storing and sharing personal data, including health information.

question: How should you correct a mistake in a handwritten care record?
optionB: Tear out the page and rewrite it
optionD: Scribble over it until it is hidden
explanation: The original entry must stay readable. Draw a single line through it, write the correction, and sign or initial and date it.

question: Which of these makes a care record entry good?
optionA: Written at the end of the week
optionC: Written in pencil to edit later
explanation: Records should be accurate, factual, legible, written promptly and dated, timed and signed so others can rely on them.

question: Where should paper care records be kept when not in use?
explanation: Records containing personal information must be stored securely so only authorised people can see them.

question: You think a care record may have been seen by someone who should not have seen it. What should you do?
optionA: Wait to see if anyone complains
optionC: Tell the person it was nothing
optionD: Delete the record to be safe
explanation: A possible data breach must be reported straight away so the organisation can assess it. Breaches that put people's rights at risk must be reported to the Information Commissioner's Office within 72 hours of the organisation becoming aware.

question: Who has the right to ask to see the information held about them?
explanation: People have the right to access their own personal data, known as a subject access request. Others need a lawful reason and proper authorisation.

question: What is good practice for a password to an electronic care record?
optionA: Write it on the screen edge
optionB: Share it with the shift team
optionC: Use the same one as a colleague
explanation: Passwords protect personal data. Keep yours private, log out when you finish and report anyone using your login.

question: A caller says they are a person's daughter and asks about their health. What should you do?
optionB: Tell them everything they ask about
optionC: Hang up the phone without speaking
optionD: Give them a brief update anyway
explanation: You cannot confirm a caller's identity by phone alone. Follow agreed ways of working, check the person's consent and who is authorised before sharing anything.

question: Why is it important to record care accurately?
optionA: So you look busy on each shift
optionB: So others can give safe care
optionC: So any mistakes can be hidden
explanation: Accurate records tell the next worker what happened and what is needed, and give legal evidence of care.

question: Which of these is a secure way to handle information on a phone used for work?
optionA: Text details on your own phone
optionB: Post updates in a group chat
optionC: Use only the approved work app
explanation: Use only systems your employer has approved. Personal phones and messaging groups risk data being lost or seen by the wrong people.

question: A person has limited speech. How could you check what they want for lunch?
explanation: Showing real food or picture cards lets the person point to their choice, supporting their communication and independence.

question: How much fluid does NHS guidance suggest most adults drink each day?
explanation: The NHS Eatwell Guide suggests 6 to 8 cups or glasses of fluid a day, more in hot weather or when active. Water, lower-fat milk and sugar-free drinks all count.

question: Which of these is a sign of dehydration?
explanation: Signs include dark concentrated urine, thirst, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, headache and, in older people, new confusion.

question: Why are older people at higher risk of dehydration?
explanation: Thirst sensation often reduces with age, and some people limit drinks to avoid needing the toilet. Offer drinks regularly rather than waiting to be asked.

question: What is the Eatwell Guide?
optionB: A daily menu for care homes
optionD: A model of a balanced diet
explanation: The Eatwell Guide shows the proportions of food groups that make up a healthy balanced diet, such as fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates.

question: A person's food and fluid chart shows they have drunk much less than usual for two days. What should you do?
explanation: Changes in intake must be reported promptly so the person can be assessed. Standard 8 asks workers to identify and report changes in nutrition and hydration needs.

question: What should you do if a person coughs and splutters every time they drink?
optionB: Report it as a swallowing risk
optionC: Stop all fluids for a day
optionD: Offer a straw without asking them
explanation: Coughing when drinking can be a sign of dysphagia, a swallowing difficulty. Report it so it can be assessed, often by a speech and language therapist.

question: What is IDDSI used for?
explanation: The International Dysphagia Diet Standardisation Initiative sets levels for drink thickness and food texture for people with swallowing difficulties.

question: What position is safest for a person to eat in?
explanation: Sitting upright, ideally at a table, helps safe swallowing and reduces the risk of choking. Follow any specific advice in the care plan.

question: A person is on a soft and bite-sized diet but asks for a crusty roll. What should you do first?
optionB: Give it to them as they asked
optionD: Cut it into small pieces for them
explanation: The texture is in the care plan for safety. Explain why, respect the person's views and involve a senior, who can review risk and choice.

question: Why must you wash your hands before helping someone eat?
optionA: To warm the food more quickly
optionC: To make the meal look better
explanation: Hand hygiene before handling food or helping someone eat reduces the spread of germs that cause food poisoning and infection.

question: What should you check first when you find a person collapsed?
optionC: That it is safe for you
explanation: Check for danger before you approach so you do not become a casualty. Then check for a response and for normal breathing.

question: How long should you take to check whether an unresponsive adult is breathing normally?
explanation: Resuscitation Council UK guidelines say to check for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Occasional gasps are not normal breathing.

question: An adult is unresponsive and not breathing normally. What should happen first?
optionB: Give them a drink of water
optionC: Wait for them to wake up
optionD: Sit them up in a chair
explanation: Call for an ambulance and ask someone to bring a defibrillator (AED) if one is available, then start chest compressions.

question: What ratio of chest compressions to rescue breaths is used for adult CPR?
explanation: Adult CPR in the UK uses 30 compressions then 2 rescue breaths. If you are unable or unwilling to give breaths, give continuous compressions.

question: At what rate should chest compressions be given in adult CPR?
explanation: Compressions should be given at 100 to 120 a minute, to a depth of 5 to 6 cm in an adult, letting the chest come back up fully each time.

question: How deep should chest compressions be for an adult?
explanation: UK guidelines advise 5 to 6 cm in an adult, in the centre of the chest, with full recoil between compressions.

question: An adult who is choking cannot cough or speak. What should you give first?
explanation: For severe choking give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts if needed, and call 999 if it is not cleared.

question: An unresponsive person is breathing normally and has no injuries that stop you moving them. How should you leave them while you wait for help?
explanation: The recovery position keeps the airway open and lets fluid drain from the mouth. Keep checking their breathing until help arrives.

question: When should you use an AED during CPR?
optionB: Only if a doctor is there
explanation: Switch on the AED and follow its spoken instructions as soon as it arrives. Keep pauses in compressions as short as possible.

question: What must you have before you give basic life support at work?
optionB: A first aid kit with a mask
explanation: Standard 12 requires practical basic life support training that meets current Resuscitation Council UK guidelines. Any person can start CPR in an emergency.

question: Which is the most common type of dementia in the UK?
explanation: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia. Vascular dementia, caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, is the second most common.

question: Which of these can be an early sign of dementia?
optionA: A sudden rash on the arms
explanation: Early signs include problems with recent memory, finding words, planning, orientation and changes in mood. Report any changes you notice.

question: How does delirium usually differ from dementia?
optionA: It develops slowly over many years
explanation: Delirium is a sudden change in confusion or alertness, often caused by infection, dehydration or medicines. It needs urgent reporting because the cause can often be treated.

question: A person with dementia keeps asking to go home to see her mother, who died years ago. What is the best approach?
optionA: Remind her firmly that her mother died
optionC: Tell her she is going home later
explanation: Repeating painful news can cause fresh grief. Acknowledge the feelings behind the words, talk about her mother and offer comfort and distraction.

question: What does "reasonable adjustments" mean?
optionB: Rules that apply to everyone the same
optionC: Cuts to care hours when budgets are tight
optionD: Changes staff make for their own ease
explanation: Under the Equality Act 2010 services must make reasonable adjustments so disabled people, including those with dementia, a learning disability or autism, are not put at a disadvantage.

question: Which of these is a common mental health condition?
explanation: Anxiety and depression are among the most common mental health conditions. Others include bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.

question: Which of these could be a sign of depression?
explanation: Signs include low mood, loss of interest, tiredness, changes in sleep and appetite, and withdrawal. Report changes so the person can get support.

question: Which law allows some people to be assessed and treated in hospital for a mental disorder without their agreement?
explanation: The Mental Health Act 1983 sets out when people can be detained, often called being sectioned, for assessment and treatment of a mental disorder.

question: Why is early diagnosis of dementia helpful?
optionD: It means care is not needed
explanation: There is no cure, but early diagnosis gives access to support and some treatments and lets people plan, for example by making a lasting power of attorney.

question: How can the environment help a person living with dementia?
explanation: Good lighting, clear signage, contrasting colours and familiar objects help orientation. Busy patterns and reflections can confuse or distress.

question: What is a learning disability?
optionA: A short illness that passes in time
optionC: A lifelong reduced ability to learn
optionD: A reading difficulty such as dyslexia
explanation: A learning disability affects the way a person understands information, learns new skills and copes independently. It starts before adulthood and is lifelong. Dyslexia is a learning difficulty, not a learning disability.

question: What is autism?
optionA: An illness that can be cured
explanation: Autism is a lifelong developmental difference affecting how people communicate, interact and process the world. Some autistic people also have a learning disability, but many do not.

question: Which of these is a common sensory difference for autistic people?
optionD: Seeing only in black and white
explanation: Many autistic people are over- or under-sensitive to sounds, lights, smells, touch or tastes. Reducing sensory overload can prevent distress.

question: What is the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training?
explanation: The Health and Care Act 2022 requires CQC-registered providers to make sure staff get learning disability and autism training suited to their role. The Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training is the standardised training the government recommends for this.

question: An autistic man becomes distressed when his daily routine changes. What helps most?
optionB: Not telling him until it happens
optionD: Asking him to just cope with it
explanation: Predictability matters to many autistic people. Give advance warning of changes, use clear language or visual aids and follow his care plan.

question: What does STOMP aim to do?
explanation: STOMP stands for stopping over-medication of people with a learning disability, autism or both, especially psychotropic medicines used to manage behaviour.

question: What is diagnostic overshadowing?
optionC: Taking a long time to diagnose
explanation: Diagnostic overshadowing happens when new symptoms are wrongly put down to a learning disability, autism or mental illness, so real health problems are missed.

question: What is a hospital passport?
optionA: An ID card for entering wards
optionB: A guide to the person's needs
explanation: A hospital passport gives staff key information about a person with a learning disability or autism: how they communicate, their needs, likes and dislikes.

question: From what age can people on their GP's learning disability register have a free annual health check in England?
explanation: People aged 14 and over on the GP learning disability register are entitled to an annual health check, which helps spot health problems early.

question: How should you communicate with a person with a learning disability?
optionA: Speak quickly to keep their interest
optionC: Talk to their carer, not them
explanation: Use clear, simple language, one idea at a time, visual aids where helpful and check the person has understood. Speak to the person directly.

question: Which statement about autism is accurate?
optionB: All autistic people avoid eye contact
explanation: Autism is a spectrum and affects people in very different ways. Generalisations lead to poor support; get to know the individual.

question: What is the social model of disability?
optionA: A person's condition is the problem
explanation: The social model says people are disabled by barriers in attitudes, buildings and systems, not by their impairment, so removing barriers is the focus.

question: A person with a mental health condition is talking about ending their life. What should you do?
optionA: Change the subject to cheer them
optionB: Promise to keep it a secret
optionC: Stay with them and get help
optionD: Wait to see if they mean it
explanation: Take any talk of suicide seriously. Stay with the person, listen and get urgent help from a senior or emergency services as your agreed ways of working say.

question: Why can a person with dementia become distressed in the late afternoon or evening?
explanation: Increased confusion and distress later in the day, sometimes called sundowning, can be linked to tiredness, changing light, hunger or unmet needs.

question: Which law sets out the duties of councils in England to safeguard adults at risk?
explanation: The Care Act 2014 puts adult safeguarding on a legal footing, including the council's duty to make enquiries, known as section 42 enquiries.

question: Under the Care Act 2014, which of these is part of the definition of an adult at risk?
optionA: They live alone and are over 75
optionB: They have care and support needs
explanation: Safeguarding duties apply to an adult who has needs for care and support, is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and as a result of those needs cannot protect themselves.

question: Which of these is one of the six safeguarding principles in the Care Act statutory guidance?
explanation: The six principles are empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership and accountability.

question: What does "Making Safeguarding Personal" mean?
optionA: Each worker keeps their own safeguarding file
optionC: Safeguarding is handled only by police
explanation: Making Safeguarding Personal means involving the person, asking what outcomes they want and supporting them to make choices about their own safety.

question: A resident's savings are being spent by a relative without her agreement. What type of abuse could this be?
explanation: Financial or material abuse includes theft, fraud, pressure over wills or money, and misuse of property or benefits.

question: Which of these is a possible sign of physical abuse?
explanation: Unexplained bruises, burns or injuries, or injuries in different stages of healing, may be signs of physical abuse and must be reported.

question: A service keeps strict routines that suit staff, such as everyone in bed by 8 pm. What type of abuse could this be?
explanation: Organisational or institutional abuse is poor care or rigid routines across a service that put staff convenience before people's needs and choices.

question: Which of these is an example of neglect?
explanation: Neglect and acts of omission include ignoring medical or physical care needs, withholding medicines, food or heating.

question: What is self-neglect?
optionA: Not caring for one's own health
explanation: Self-neglect covers a wide range of behaviour where a person does not care for their own hygiene, health or surroundings, including hoarding.

question: Which of these is a type of abuse listed in the Care Act statutory guidance?
explanation: The guidance lists physical, domestic, sexual, psychological, financial or material, modern slavery, discriminatory, organisational, neglect and acts of omission, and self-neglect.

question: A person tells you a staff member has been hurting them. What should you do?
optionA: Promise to keep it a secret
optionB: Ask the staff member about it
explanation: Listen calmly, take it seriously, do not promise secrecy, do not investigate yourself, and report straight away following your safeguarding policy.

question: When a person discloses abuse, what kind of questions should you avoid?
explanation: Leading questions can suggest answers and affect any later investigation. Let the person speak, and record what they say in their own words.

question: How should you record a disclosure of abuse?
optionB: In your summary of what happened
optionD: A week later when it is calm
explanation: Record what was said using the person's own words, what you saw, the date and time and who you reported to. Keep to facts, not opinions.

question: What should you do if you report a safeguarding concern and nothing seems to be done?
optionA: Drop it as you have done your part
optionB: Escalate it to a higher level
explanation: If a concern is not acted on, escalate it to a senior manager, the local authority safeguarding team or CQC. Whistleblowing law protects workers who raise concerns in the right way.

question: Which law protects workers who report wrongdoing at work in the public interest?
optionD: The Health and Social Care Act 2008
explanation: The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who make a qualifying disclosure, often called whistleblowing, from unfair treatment.

question: Which is an example of a restrictive practice?
optionB: Helping someone get to a club
optionD: Locking a door to keep someone in
explanation: Restrictive practices limit a person's movement or freedom. They must be lawful, proportionate, the least restrictive option and recorded.

question: A person is being pressured online by someone asking for money. What risk is this?
explanation: Technology brings risks such as scams, online grooming and exploitation. The 2025 standards expanded coverage of technology-related risks.

question: Who should you first report a safeguarding concern to at work?
optionC: A reporter at the local paper
explanation: Follow your safeguarding policy, which normally means reporting to your manager or the named safeguarding lead. If they are involved, go to the local authority or CQC.

question: Up to what age is a person classed as a child for safeguarding purposes in England?
explanation: Everyone under 18 is a child for child protection purposes, even if they live independently or are in work.

question: Which statutory guidance sets out how agencies in England work together to protect children?
optionB: The Care and Support Statutory Guidance
explanation: Working Together to Safeguard Children is the statutory guidance on inter-agency working to safeguard and promote the welfare of children.

question: You visit an adult at home and see that a child there seems frightened and has burns. What should you do?
optionB: Leave it, you only support adults
optionC: Ask the child to show you
explanation: Everyone who works with adults or children has a responsibility to safeguard children. Report concerns about a child promptly using agreed procedures.

question: Which of these is a type of child abuse?
explanation: The main categories are physical, emotional and sexual abuse and neglect. Child exploitation and online abuse also fall within them.

question: Which of these is a sign that a child may be neglected?
optionA: Has a few untidy toys at home
explanation: Signs of neglect include persistent hunger, poor hygiene, clothes unsuited to the weather, missed health appointments and being left alone.

question: If you think a child is in immediate danger, what should you do?
explanation: If a child or adult is in immediate danger, call the police on 999. Then follow your organisation's procedures.

question: What is the safest attitude to take about who might abuse someone?
explanation: Abuse can be carried out by anyone, including family, friends, staff, volunteers and other people using services. Keep an open mind.

question: What should you do if someone you suspect of abuse asks you what was reported?
optionA: Show them a copy of the report
optionC: Warn them to stop what they do
explanation: Telling the alleged abuser could put the person at further risk or affect an investigation. Pass the approach on to your manager.

question: Which of these is psychological abuse?
explanation: Psychological abuse includes threats, humiliation, controlling behaviour, intimidation, isolation and verbal abuse.

question: Which type of abuse involves treating someone badly because of their race or disability?
explanation: Discriminatory abuse includes harassment, slurs or unequal treatment because of a protected characteristic such as race, disability, age or sexuality.

question: Which law sets out the main duties of employers and employees for health and safety at work in Great Britain?
optionA: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
optionC: The Health and Social Care Act 2008
explanation: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 places duties on employers to protect staff and others, and on employees to take reasonable care and cooperate.

question: What is one of your own duties as an employee under health and safety law?
optionA: Write the risk assessments for the home
explanation: Employees must take reasonable care of their own health and safety and that of others, cooperate with their employer and use equipment as trained.

question: What is the correct order for managing a manual handling task?
explanation: Under the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 employers should avoid hazardous manual handling where possible, assess what cannot be avoided and reduce the risk.

question: Before using a hoist, what should you check?
optionA: Only that the battery light is on
optionB: That a relative is there to watch
optionC: That the person has eaten recently
optionD: The sling and hoist are right and safe
explanation: Check you are trained, the care plan says which hoist and sling to use, the equipment is in date for inspection and undamaged, and the person consents.

question: Which regulations require hoists used for lifting people to be thoroughly examined at set intervals?
explanation: The Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 (LOLER) require thorough examination of lifting equipment; equipment for lifting people is examined at least every six months.

question: What does COSHH cover?
explanation: The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 cover substances such as cleaning chemicals. Use and store them as the data sheet and risk assessment say.

question: What does RIDDOR require?
explanation: The Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013 require employers to report specified injuries, diseases and dangerous occurrences to the enforcing authority.

question: You find a chemical in an unlabelled bottle. What should you do?
optionC: Use it if it looks clean
optionD: Do not use it and report it
explanation: Unlabelled substances could be dangerous. Do not use or sniff them; report to your manager so they can be identified and disposed of safely.

question: Which fire extinguisher is suitable for an electrical fire?
explanation: Carbon dioxide extinguishers, with a black label, are suitable for electrical fires. Water must never be used on live electrical equipment.

question: What should you do first if you discover a fire at work?
explanation: Raise the alarm so everyone is warned and help is called, then follow your fire procedure. Only tackle a fire if trained and it is safe.

question: Which of these is a sign of stress in a care worker?
explanation: Stress can show as poor sleep, irritability, tiredness, headaches and difficulty concentrating. Spotting your own triggers helps you seek support early.

question: Where can a care worker get support with work-related stress?
optionC: Nowhere, it is part of the job
optionD: Their manager or a support line
explanation: Talk to your manager, use supervision and any employee assistance service, and see your GP if needed. Stress affects safety as well as wellbeing.

question: Which link comes first in the six-link chain of infection?
explanation: The chain runs: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Breaking any link stops the spread.

question: What is the single most important way to prevent the spread of infection?
explanation: Hand hygiene at the right moments is the most effective way to prevent infections spreading between people.

question: How long should a thorough handwash with soap and water take?
explanation: A full handwash takes about 40 to 60 seconds, covering all parts of the hands. An alcohol hand rub takes about 20 to 30 seconds.

question: When is alcohol hand rub not enough, so you must wash with soap and water?
optionA: After touching a clean table top
optionC: After filling in a care chart
optionD: After care for someone with diarrhoea
explanation: Alcohol rub does not work well against Clostridioides difficile spores or norovirus, and does not clean visibly dirty hands. Use soap and water.

question: In what order should you put on an apron, mask and gloves?
explanation: Put on the apron first, then the mask or respirator and eye protection, and gloves last. Gloves are removed first because they are the most contaminated.

question: Which item of PPE should you take off first?
explanation: Gloves are the most contaminated, so they come off first, then the apron, then eye protection and finally the mask. Clean your hands afterwards.

question: Why should you not wear a wristwatch or long sleeves during personal care?
optionA: They are too expensive to risk
optionD: They break PPE rules on colour
explanation: Being bare below the elbows lets you wash hands and wrists properly and stops germs being carried on cuffs and jewellery.

question: How should you deal with a small blood spill in a care home?
optionA: Wipe it with a dry paper towel
optionB: Cover it and leave it for later
optionC: Mop it up with the floor mop
optionD: Wear PPE and use the spill kit
explanation: Follow the spill procedure: wear gloves and an apron, use the spill kit or the disinfectant your policy sets, then dispose of waste as clinical waste and clean your hands.

question: What should you do with a used needle?
optionA: Put it straight in a sharps bin
optionB: Recap it before putting it away
optionC: Put it in a clinical waste bag
optionD: Leave it on the tray for a nurse
explanation: Dispose of sharps immediately at the point of use into a sharps container, without recapping. Do not fill the bin above the fill line.

question: What should you do straight away after a needlestick injury?
optionA: Suck the wound to clean it
optionB: Let it bleed and wash it
optionC: Scrub it with a nail brush
optionD: Cover it and carry on working
explanation: Encourage it to bleed without sucking it, wash with running water and soap, cover it, then report it urgently so you can be assessed.

question: How should linen soiled with body fluids be handled?
optionB: Rinsed by hand in the sink first
optionC: In a dissolvable bag in a red bag
explanation: Infectious or soiled linen goes in a water-soluble (alginate) bag inside an outer bag, usually red, so it can go into the washer without being handled again. Never shake it.

question: Which of these breaks the chain of infection at the portal of entry?
optionA: Putting soiled waste in a bin
optionD: Covering a cut with a dressing
explanation: Covering broken skin stops germs getting in. Cleaning equipment removes the reservoir, and isolation reduces transmission.

question: What is a healthcare-associated infection?
optionB: An infection a person had at birth
optionC: An infection only staff can catch
explanation: A healthcare-associated infection develops as a result of care or treatment in any setting, such as a urine infection from a catheter.

question: Why is cleaning a commode after each use important?
optionA: It makes it lighter to move
optionD: It keeps it warm for use
explanation: Cleaning and disinfecting shared equipment between uses removes the reservoir of germs and stops infections spreading between people.

question: You have diarrhoea and vomiting before a shift. What should you do?
optionA: Work but wear gloves all day
optionB: Work if you feel well enough
optionC: Stay off and tell your manager
optionD: Take medicine and go in anyway
explanation: Staff with diarrhoea or vomiting should stay away from work until symptom free for 48 hours, as set out in infection control guidance, to avoid spreading illness.

question: Which waste usually goes in an orange clinical waste bag?
explanation: Orange bags are for infectious clinical waste. Bag colours and rules depend on the setting, so follow your waste policy.
